evidence_set: Kentucky has a hybrid system in which elected county coroners investigate and certify cause and manner of death in coroner cases, with or without referral for autopsy to one of four regional medical examiner offices; the state medical examiner's office funds all toxicology testing. Eligibility for the office is age 24, one year's residence in the county and two in the state, with no training in medicine or forensic pathology required; newly elected coroners must complete 40 hours of basic death-investigation training. Of 48 responding coroners, 47 (98%) held another position, 28 (58.3%) as funeral directors.

evidence_set: How a case entered the pooled data: an individually described case of 'excited delirium' or 'agitated delirium' in an English-language case report or series found in PubMed/Ovid Medline and Google Scholar to 23 April 2020 (cases the reviewers deemed neither were excluded); outcome recorded as survival or death as the source reported it; neither label is in ICD-9, ICD-10 or DSM-5; the diagnosis was coded by the reviewers from the term used in the article; drug intoxication was coded in categories from the most commonly described toxicities, with no toxicology results or concentrations extracted.

The authors note that the forensic-pathology literature almost exclusively uses 'excited delirium' and describes only deaths, while the clinical literature uses both terms for the same presentation and includes survivors as well as deaths, and that deaths are more likely to be published and better documented (toxicology, police reports, witnesses); the first reader's appraisal is that this split ties the label, death and the recording of restraint together through the type of source, which the analysis (univariate tests only) did not stratify or adjust for.
